question: Who's ahead in the Texas Senate race?

answer.text:
Talarico (D) leads Paxton (R) 50% to 44% among Texas registered voters in the Marist Poll, with 2% choosing another candidate and 4% undecided. The poll was conducted September 17–20, 2026, with 1,139 registered voters and a margin of error of ±4.4 points.

The 6-point lead is only a little larger than the margin of error. Marist says Talarico has majority support among independents (55%). Even so, 52% of voters overall think Paxton will win the race.

question: What share of Americans say the Trump administration is doing too much on deportations?

answer.text:
52% of U.S. adults say the Trump administration is doing too much to deport immigrants living in the country illegally, according to a Pew Research Center survey of 3,592 adults conducted April 6-12, 2026. That is little changed from October 2025. Pew's chart puts the October figure at 53%.

The survey's margin of error is ±1.9 points.

Other findings:
- 31% say the administration is doing about the right amount, and 15% say too little.
- 84% of Democrats and Democratic leaners say it is doing too much, compared with 19% of Republicans and Republican leaners.

question: Will Democrats win the House in November?

answer.text:

- **Voter expectations:** 52% of registered voters think the Democrat in their district will win, while 44% think the Republican will.
- **Trump as a factor:** 45% call their congressional vote mostly a vote against President Trump, compared with 24% who call it mostly a vote for him. His job approval rating remains under 40%.

These are national polls from a single pollster, mostly Marist. They don't translate into a seat count, and the results here don't include district-level races or a forecast model. The Democratic lead has been steady, but the polls can't tell you the outcome.

Midterm Elections in Ohio, September 2026
Democrats Lead in Ohio's Senate & Gubernatorial Contests... Impressions of Trump Loom Large

Ohio registered voters approach the midterm election cycle with a sour mood toward President Donald Trump and lean Democratic in the state’s marquee contests. In the race for U.S. Senate in Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown has an eight-point advantage against Republican Jon Husted, and the Democrats are +3 against the Republicans on the generic congressional ballot question. In the state’s gubernatorial contest, Democrat Amy Acton leads Republican Vivek Ramaswamy by six points. President Trump’s lackluster approval rating in Ohio and voters’ downtrodden views of their personal finances underpin the electoral landscape.

Survey details: Fielded 2026-09-24 to 2026-09-27; 1,298 registered voters; geography OH; margin of error ±3.8 points.

Trump Loses Ground on Several Personal Traits as Approval Rating Slips
How Trump’s 2024 voters evaluate his job performance

Trump’s approval rating has also declined substantially among those who did not vote in 2024: 26% of these U.S. adults now approve of his job performance, down from 30% in January and 45% in early 2025.

Nearly all 2024 Kamala Harris voters (98%) disapprove of Trump’s job performance, little changed over the course of his term.

Survey details: Fielded 2026-04-20 to 2026-04-26; 5,103 adults; geography US; margin of error ±1.6 points.

Midterm voting preferences by race, age and other demographics

Voters 30 to 49 also prefer Democratic candidates by 42% to 35%. While in most recent elections voters in this age group have tended to back Democratic candidates, those who turned out in the 2024 presidential election split their votes about evenly between Donald Trump and Kamala Harris.

Among those 50 to 64, 44% prefer a Republican candidate, while 39% prefer a Democratic candidate.

Paralleling patterns in partisan identification, college graduates are much more likely than those without a bachelor’s degree to back Democratic candidates.

By about two-to-one, those with a graduate degree prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans (59% to 29%). By a more modest margin, those with a bachelor’s degree but without a higher degree also back Democrats (48% to 35%).

Survey details: Fielded 2026-07-06 to 2026-07-12; 3,554 adults; geography US; margin of error ±1.9 points.

Midterm Elections in Ohio, September 2026
Democrats Lead in Ohio's Senate & Gubernatorial Contests... Impressions of Trump Loom Large

A plurality of Ohio voters (41%) say their congressional vote is mainly a vote against President Trump. 25% say it is a vote for the president, and 33% report President Trump is not much of a factor when considering their vote. Of those Ohio voters who say the president is not influencing their vote, a majority approve of how President Trump is doing his job.

Acton (50%) leads Ramaswamy (44%) in Ohio's gubernatorial contest among registered voters statewide. Among independents, 57% back Acton compared with 32% for Ramaswamy. However, when asked which candidate they think will actually win, Ramaswamy (53%) has the advantage over Acton (43%).

Survey details: Fielded 2026-09-24 to 2026-09-27; 1,298 registered voters; geography OH; margin of error ±3.8 points.

2026 Midterm Elections, September 2026
Voters Confident in Fair Elections & USPS; Fewer Trust Validity of Mail-In Ballots

Voters express confidence in the mechanics of the election, itself. 75% are either very confident or confident that their state or local government will run a fair and accurate election. This includes 86% of Democrats. 66% of Republicans, and 74% of independents. The proportion of voters who express confidence in the election process is up from 69% in March.

Voters (58%) also trust that the United States Postal Service will deliver election-related mail to voters and election officials in a timely way. However, there has been a significant drop in confidence since 2024 when 71% of registered voters reported they trusteed the USPS to deliver election-related material. Regardless of political affiliation, a majority has a high degree of confidence in the USPS.

Survey details: Fielded 2026-09-14 to 2026-09-15; 1,280 registered voters; geography US; margin of error ±3.8 points.

As the 2026 Midterms Approach, Economy Is Front and Center
Democratic candidates hold a modest edge on the generic ballot, while their voters are more attentive to the campaign

These are among the key findings of a new Pew Research Center survey conducted from July 6 to 12 among 3,554 U.S. adults, including 2,779 registered voters. The survey also finds that President Donald Trump looms large in the campaign. Most voters say the president is a factor in their vote – though by roughly two-to-one, voters are more likely to say they think of their vote this fall as a vote against Trump (42%) than to say they think of it as a vote for him (22%).

Views of Trump are a bigger factor for voters today than views of then-President Joe Biden were at a similar point four years ago.

Survey details: Fielded 2026-07-06 to 2026-07-12; 3,554 adults; geography US; margin of error ±1.9 points.
